transcript.content: Man in his 60s, T2DM on metformin (HbA1c 8.4), RUQ pain 3 days, T 38.4. WBC 14,200, CRP 112, bili 1.1, Cr 1.0. US: stone, wall 5 mm, CBD 5 mm. District hospital, laparoscopy available. Lap chole within 24-48 h, or antibiotics and delayed surgery at 6 weeks? It hinges on whether he is Grade I or II under TG18 at day 3. Keep to TG18 and give the source for each recommendation.

Good case to think through; the decision does hinge on the grade.
- Severity: TG18 calls it Grade II if any of these is present: WBC above 18,000, a palpable tender RUQ mass, symptoms beyond 72 h, or marked local inflammation (gangrene, abscess, biliary peritonitis). On your numbers WBC is 14,200 and there is no mass, so duration is the only criterion in play (Tokyo Guidelines, 2018).
- Timing: early laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the preferred route for Grade I, and it shortens total hospital stay without raising complications compared with delayed surgery (Tokyo Guidelines, 2018).
- Antibiotics and a wait of about 6 weeks is the fallback for patients who cannot have early surgery, not the default.
❓ Where exactly do you start the 72 hours, and what finding would push him from Grade I to Grade II?

You put the 72 h line right at the edge for him. Leading hypothesis is simple cholecystitis, Grade I, because WBC is only 14,200, no mass, wall 5 mm. Second is early gangrenous change, given CRP 112 and T 38.4. Third is a duct stone, less likely with bili 1.1 and CBD 5 mm. I will repeat US and CRP at 12 h to separate the first two.

Both readings are reasonable, and gangrenous change is the one that matters.
- Marked local inflammation is itself a Grade II criterion, so a thicker wall or a CRP that keeps climbing at 12 h reclassifies him (Tokyo Guidelines, 2018).
- Date the 72 hours from the onset of the pain that brought him in, and note how you dated it in the chart.
- For Grade II, TG18 supports early LC only in a centre with advanced laparoscopic experience when there are no negative predictors (jaundice, neurological or respiratory dysfunction); otherwise drain first (Tokyo Guidelines, 2018).
- I'm not certain of the exact number of days after onset that TG18 gives as the outer limit for early surgery; the usual teaching is within about a week.
❓ If the repeat ultrasound shows a thicker wall but his CRP is flat, which finding would you trust more?

Back to the shorter-stay claim in your first answer. Sorting it:
1. Early LC beats delayed on total stay: several RCTs, but mostly Grade I-II patients, surgeons who do laparoscopy daily.
2. Grade II negative-predictor list: consensus opinion, no trial I know of.
3. Diabetic man, HbA1c 8.4, 1 surgeon on call: no source I know of tested that mix.
Please say which of the three you cannot source.

Fair challenge, and you have sorted it correctly.
- The shorter-stay result came from trials that mostly enrolled Grade I-II patients, with surgeons experienced in laparoscopy and few high-risk patients, so I stated it without its edges (Tokyo Guidelines, 2018).
- The negative-predictor list rests on expert consensus rather than a trial, and your third point stands: I know of no trial of this exact mix.
- Your sourcing note is a good habit; the evidence for high-risk patients is mainly observational.
❓ Given that, what would you ask the theatre team before fixing the first list?

Repeat at 12 h: CRP 131, wall 6 mm, T 37.9. I said Grade I earlier; with CRP up from 112 and the wall thicker, I now rank gangrenous change level with simple cholecystitis, so I treat him as borderline Grade II. First list is about 30 h from admission. Glucose 246 on arrival; metformin held, sliding-scale insulin, checks every 4 h. Which glucose range should I reach before induction?

Reasonable plan; metformin held and insulin cover are standard for a surgical admission.
- Aim for glucose 100-180 mg/dL around surgery (ADA Standards of Care, 2024).
- An HbA1c of 8.4 is not a reason to delay an urgent operation, but it raises the risk of wound infection, so check glucose every 4 h and keep it in range after surgery too.
- Antibiotics continue until surgery; keep him nil by mouth from midnight.
❓ If the 12 h repeat had been flat rather than rising, would you still have moved him to borderline Grade II?

Plan, written by me: lap chole on the first list at 08:00, antibiotics until then, glucose 100-180 mg/dL before induction, consent includes conversion. Gangrenous gallbladder means convert or drain. Check this list against TG18 only and name the section for anything that contradicts it. I will read that section myself too, since you were not sure of the day limit.

Nothing in your list contradicts TG18.
- Bail-out options when the gallbladder is gangrenous or the anatomy is unsafe (conversion, drainage, subtotal cholecystectomy) are all set out in the TG18 surgical strategy section (Tokyo Guidelines, 2018).
- The glucose range matches the ADA perioperative target (ADA Standards of Care, 2024).
- I can't give you the day limit with confidence, so reading the timing section yourself is the right move.
❓ If the first list is cancelled and he waits a further 24 h, which finding would make you reach for drainage rather than waiting for the next list?

เรียนรู้อะไร / What I learned:
I came in treating 72 hours as a hard line. It is one Grade II marker among several, and the early-surgery results I leaned on came from patients and surgeons unlike mine. I now grade him on the whole picture and re-check at 12 hours.

ความไม่แน่นอน / What remains uncertain:
Whether a diabetic man with HbA1c 8.4 and a single surgeon on call does as well as the trial groups. I also do not know our own conversion rate beyond hearsay.

จะตรวจสอบ/นำไปใช้อย่างไร / How I will verify or apply it:
Read the TG18 timing section myself, and for this patient record grade, hours from onset and what I find at surgery so the team can see how the call was made.
